title: Threat Modeling
summary: Structured methods for finding a system's weaknesses before an attacker does — data flow diagrams, STRIDE, attack trees, and risk scoring — worked through a real login flow end to end.

slides.markdown:
**Threat modeling** is the structured exercise of asking "what could go wrong here, and how" about a system's design — before it's built, not after it's breached. It turns "is this secure" (unanswerable) into a checklist of specific, falsifiable questions about a specific data flow.

This topic covers the toolkit interviewers expect you to recognize: drawing a system as a data flow diagram with trust boundaries, using STRIDE to systematically enumerate threat categories, building attack trees to decompose an attacker's goal, and scoring the results so you know what to fix first.

This is [Defense in Depth](defense-in-depth) and [Security Design Principles](security-design-principles) turned into a repeatable process: instead of applying principles from memory, you derive exactly which ones a given system needs.

slides.sectionTitle: Why you threat model before you build
slides.markdown:
Threat modeling during design finds issues that require re-architecting a data flow — the exact issues that are cheapest to fix on a whiteboard and most expensive to fix in production. Threat modeling after launch, or not at all, finds the same issues via a penetration test, a bug bounty report, or an actual incident — each progressively more expensive and more public than the last.

The cost asymmetry is the entire argument: catching "this service trusts a client-supplied user ID with no server-side check" in a design review costs an hour of discussion. Catching it after launch costs an incident response, a disclosure process, and a scramble to patch every endpoint that made the same assumption, because by then the flawed assumption is baked into dozens of call sites.

Threat modeling isn't a security team's separate task bolted onto a schedule — the strongest programs run it as a normal part of design review, the same way a team reviews for performance or scalability before shipping.

slides.sectionTitle: Data flow diagrams and trust boundaries
slides.markdown:
A **data flow diagram (DFD)** for threat modeling has four element types: **external entities** (a user, a third-party API), **processes** (your services), **data stores** (databases, caches), and **data flows** (arrows between them, labeled with what's moving).

The element that actually drives the analysis is the **trust boundary** — a line drawn wherever data crosses from one trust level to another: browser to server, one microservice to another, your infrastructure to a third-party vendor. Every threat modeling method starts by asking what happens at each boundary crossing, because that's precisely where an assumption ("this data is already validated," "this caller is already authenticated") most often turns out to be false.

Drawing the DFD is often the highest-value step of the whole exercise on its own — teams frequently discover, in the act of drawing it, a trust boundary nobody had consciously designed for: a background job that reads directly from a queue no service validates, or an internal API assumed to only be called by trusted services that's actually reachable from anywhere on the corporate network.

slides.sectionTitle: A DFD with trust boundaries, for a web app
slides.markdown:
![A data flow diagram of a login feature with three trust boundaries: browser to gateway, gateway to auth service, and auth service to database](assets/login-trust-boundaries.svg)

Notice that three of the four elements sit *behind* at least one trust boundary — which is the point. A login flow looks like a single feature from the outside, but it crosses three separate trust boundaries internally, and each one is a place where "the caller already validated this" needs to be checked rather than assumed. The next few slides walk exactly this diagram through STRIDE and a worked risk assessment.

assets.alt: A data flow diagram of a login feature with three trust boundaries: browser to gateway, gateway to auth service, and auth service to database

slides.markdown:
**STRIDE**, from Microsoft's threat modeling work, gives you six categories to check at every trust boundary and every element, so you don't rely on memory or luck to think of the right threat:

- **S**poofing — pretending to be something/someone you're not
- **T**ampering — modifying data or code without authorization
- **R**epudiation — denying you performed an action, with no way to prove otherwise
- **I**nformation disclosure — exposing data to someone unauthorized
- **D**enial of service — degrading or blocking legitimate access
- **E**levation of privilege — gaining capabilities you shouldn't have

Map this back to CIA: spoofing and repudiation relate to authentication and non-repudiation, tampering and elevation of privilege threaten integrity, information disclosure threatens confidentiality, and denial of service threatens availability directly. STRIDE's value is that it's a checklist, not a creative exercise — for each element in your DFD, you walk all six letters and ask "could this happen here," which catches threats a purely open-ended brainstorm misses.

slides.subTitle: Decomposing an attacker's goal into paths
slides.markdown:
Where STRIDE walks a diagram element by element, an **attack tree** starts from an attacker's *goal* — "take over a user's account" — as the root, and breaks it into the specific paths that could achieve it, each path a branch that can itself decompose further.

For "take over a user's account," the tree might branch into: guess or brute-force the password; phish the credential; exploit a session-fixation bug; reset the password via a compromised recovery email; or exploit a vulnerability in a federated login provider. Each of those branches decomposes further — "brute-force the password" splits into "no rate limiting exists" or "rate limiting exists but can be bypassed via distributed IPs."

Attack trees are especially useful for a specific, high-value asset where you want exhaustive coverage of every path to it, rather than a general sweep of a whole system — they complement STRIDE rather than replace it: STRIDE finds *categories* of threat systematically, attack trees find every concrete *path* to one specific outcome that matters most.

A threat model can surface dozens of theoretical threats. Not all of them deserve equal engineering time, and **risk scoring** is how you decide priority: score each threat on **likelihood** (how feasible is this attack, realistically, given required skill, access, and existing controls) and **impact** (how bad is it if it succeeds — data exposed, money lost, downtime caused), then prioritize the highest combination of both.

A threat that's high-impact but requires nation-state-level resources and physical access to a data center is usually lower priority than a medium-impact threat exploitable by anyone with a browser and no special access. This is exactly why a threat model needs scoring, not just a list — an unscored list of forty threats gets triaged by whoever's loudest or most recent, not by actual risk.

Risk scoring is where threat modeling connects to the next topic in this group: CVSS and formal risk frameworks are a more rigorous, standardized version of this same likelihood-times-impact idea, built specifically so scores are comparable across an organization rather than one team's gut feeling.

| | STRIDE | DREAD | PASTA |
|---|---|---|
| **What it does** | Enumerates threat *categories* to check per element | Scores an *already-identified* threat's severity | A full seven-stage process from business objectives to simulated attacks |
| **Question it answers** | "What kinds of things could go wrong here?" | "How bad is this specific threat, numerically?" | "What should we build, given real attacker behavior and business risk?" |
| **Best fit** | Design-time review of a specific component or feature | Quick triage/prioritization once threats are found | Larger, business-critical systems where risk needs to tie back to specific attacker TTPs |
| **Effort** | Low–medium, fits in a design review | Low — a scoring rubric applied per threat | High — a full methodology, often for compliance-heavy environments |

These aren't mutually exclusive: a common real-world combination is STRIDE to find the threats, then a DREAD-style score (or the simpler likelihood × impact from the previous slide) to prioritize them. PASTA is the heavyweight option, reserved for systems where the up-front process investment is justified by the system's criticality — most application-level threat modeling in practice is STRIDE plus a lightweight scoring pass, not full PASTA.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: threat-modeling a login flow
slides.markdown:
Applying the whole toolkit to the DFD from earlier, compressed into the threats that actually matter:

```text
Element: browser -> API gateway (trust boundary: internet -> DMZ)
  S: attacker spoofs a legitimate client -> mitigate with TLS + client validation
  D: credential-stuffing flood -> mitigate with rate limiting + CAPTCHA on repeat failures

Element: gateway -> auth service (trust boundary: DMZ -> internal network)
  T: an internal caller bypasses the gateway's rate limiting -> mitigate: auth
     service enforces its own limits too, doesn't trust the gateway alone

Element: auth service -> user database (trust boundary: internal -> data tier)
  I: a SQL injection in a legacy query path leaks password hashes -> mitigate
     with parameterized queries + least-privilege DB credential (read-only
     on the users table for this service)
  E: an attacker with a stolen session token gains admin capabilities -> mitigate
     by re-validating role on every privileged action, not caching it in the token
```

Each line follows the same shape: element, trust boundary, STRIDE category, concrete mitigation. This is what a threat model actually produces — not a security score, but a short list of specific design decisions with a reason attached to each one.

slides.sectionTitle: Threat-modeling once, at launch, and never again
slides.markdown:
A threat model produced once before launch and filed away is a snapshot of a system that no longer exists by the time it's read again. Systems change constantly — new features add new data flows, new trust boundaries appear when you integrate a third-party API, new attack techniques get published — and a threat model that isn't revisited silently goes stale.

The concrete failure this causes: a team adds a new webhook integration eighteen months after the original threat model, reuses the existing auth service without re-examining it, and misses that the new integration introduces a trust boundary (an external vendor's servers) the original model never considered, because it didn't exist yet.

The fix isn't "redo the full model constantly" — it's triggering a targeted re-review at specific events: a new external integration, a new trust boundary, a significant architecture change, or a relevant new attack technique becoming public. Threat modeling is a practice with a cadence, not a document with a completion date.

slides.sectionTitle: Threat modeling as a habit, not an event
slides.markdown:
The senior-level framing of this topic: threat modeling isn't a deliverable you produce once, it's a lens you apply repeatedly, and the specific method matters less than consistently asking the right questions at the right time.

A lightweight version that scales to a normal engineering team: for any new feature crossing a trust boundary, spend fifteen minutes drawing the data flow, walk STRIDE across the new elements, and write down the two or three highest-risk findings with a mitigation each. That's a far smaller investment than a formal PASTA exercise, and it catches the majority of design-time issues that would otherwise surface as production incidents.

The next topic, Risk, Vulnerabilities & Security Frameworks, formalizes the scoring side of this — CVSS and structured risk frameworks are what a mature organization uses to make threat-model findings comparable and prioritizable across many teams, not just one team's judgment call.
